subject: Climate & Environment
title: Hazardous Waste and Health
description: A micro-lesson that makes Hazardous Waste and Health usable.

hook.text: Every year, 300 million tons of hazardous waste are produced globally. Much of it is mismanaged.

buildup.text: Chemical plants, hospitals, and factories generate waste containing heavy metals and toxins.

discovery.text: When improperly stored, these toxins leak into groundwater and contaminate soil for decades.

twist.text: Love Canal in New York — built over a toxic dump — made residents sick for generations.

climax.text: Strict regulation works. The US Superfund program has cleaned over 400 toxic sites since 1980.

punchline.text: What we bury carelessly today, our children inherit tomorrow.

quiz.question: What was the Love Canal disaster?
options: A neighborhood built on a toxic waste dump
A chemical spill in a river

details.summary: Hazardous waste from industry, healthcare, and households includes chemicals, heavy metals, and radioactive materials that pose severe health risks. Improper disposal contaminates water, soil, and air, causing cancer, birth defects, and neurological damage in exposed communities worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Hazardous waste disproportionately harms low-income and marginalized communities. Proper management and regulation are essential for protecting public health and environmental justice.
takeaways: Hazardous waste includes chemicals, heavy metals, and radioactive material
Improper disposal causes cancer and neurological damage
Vulnerable communities bear the greatest health burden

faq.question: What counts as hazardous waste?
faq.answer: Waste is classified hazardous if it is ignitable, corrosive, reactive, or toxic. Examples include industrial solvents, pesticides, battery acid, medical sharps, asbestos, and electronics containing lead or mercury. Specific definitions vary by country and regulation.

faq.question: Where is hazardous waste most often dumped illegally?
faq.answer: Illegal dumping concentrates in countries with weak enforcement, often in Africa and Southeast Asia. The Probo Koala incident in 2006, where toxic waste from a Dutch company was dumped in Ivory Coast, sickened over 100,000 people and highlighted regulatory failures.
